title: Docker Networking
intro: Containers on different networks can't see each other by default, even on the same machine — this is the single most common cause of 'my app can't connect to my database' in local Docker setups.

steps.prompt: List the networks that currently exist.
steps.fake_output:
NETWORK ID     NAME      DRIVER    SCOPE
abc123def456   bridge    bridge    local
def456abc789   host      host      local
012345678901   none      null      local
steps.explanation: 'bridge' is the default network new containers join if you don't specify one — but two containers both on the default bridge still can't reliably reach each other by container name.
steps.why: Compose creates its own dedicated network automatically (as seen in the Compose tutorial) specifically to avoid this default-bridge limitation — 'docker network ls' is how you'd confirm that network actually exists when debugging a Compose networking issue.

steps.prompt: Create a custom bridge network called 'app-net'.
steps.explanation: Containers on a custom network can resolve each other by container name automatically — this is the built-in DNS the default bridge network doesn't give you.
steps.why: This is the manual equivalent of what Compose does for you automatically — worth knowing directly for the times you're running plain 'docker run' rather than Compose.

steps.prompt: Run a postgres container named 'db' attached to that network.
steps.explanation: Now any other container on 'app-net' can reach this one at the hostname 'db' — no IP address needed.
steps.why: Naming the container matters here specifically because that name becomes the DNS hostname other containers use — an auto-generated random name would still work, but 'db' is far more predictable to reference from your app's connection string.

steps.prompt: Run your app container on the same network so it can reach 'db'.
steps.explanation: Both containers being on 'app-net' is what makes 'db' resolvable from inside 'web' — if you forgot --network here, this exact setup would silently fail to connect.
steps.why: This is the fix for the most common Docker networking mistake: two containers meant to talk to each other, started with plain 'docker run' and no shared --network, ending up isolated from one another by default.

steps.prompt: Inspect the network to see exactly which containers are attached to it.
steps.explanation: This is the direct way to confirm two containers are actually on the same network — the first thing to check when 'connection refused' turns out to be a networking issue, not an app bug.
steps.why: 'docker inspect <container>' also shows a container's own network info, but only for that one container — 'network inspect' shows everyone attached to a given network at once, which is faster when you're checking whether two specific containers can actually see each other.
